question: My rent app charges a fee when I pay by card. There's also a manual bank transfer option with no fee, but it's slower. Can the app charge me the card fee? Does it matter whether the fee goes to the app company or to the agent?
answer:
**Short answer:** Based on the retrieved documents, the card fee is very likely not allowed. Whether the fee goes to the app or the agent doesn't change that, because the main prohibition applies to "a person," not just the agent. The documents don't cover whether a slower payment method is acceptable.

**Which law applies:** The Residential Tenancies Act 1997 is in Authorised Version No. 115, in force from 13 October 2026 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 are in Authorised Version No. 009, in force from 30 June 2026 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

## What the law says

- **Fees for paying rent are prohibited.** A person, other than an ADI, must not demand or receive a fee for any prescribed matter in relation to the payment of rent. The penalty is 80 penalty units for a natural person or 400 penalty units for a body corporate [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The Regulations prescribe "rent payment (other than payment surcharge fees permitted under any other Act)" as a prohibited matter [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). I couldn't find any other Act in the retrieved material that permits a payment surcharge, so I can't say whether that exception applies to your app.
- **The only fee-free exception is your own bank fees.** A no-additional-cost payment method must be reasonably available to you. The rental provider or agent must ensure this, other than for bank fees or account fees on your bank account [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). A card fee charged by an app is not one of those bank or account fees.
- **Electronic payment fees are prohibited.** A person must not demand or receive a charge for establishing or using direct debit or another electronic payment facility for rent [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Rent terms requiring a costly payment method are prohibited.** A term requiring rent to be paid in advance by a payment method with additional costs (other than bank or account fees) is a prohibited term [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **Costs must be disclosed first.** The provider or agent must tell you about any costs, including third-party transaction fees, before you consent to a payment method [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

## Does it matter who gets the fee?

Under the documents, it doesn't matter for the fee prohibition. Section 51A applies to "a person" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf), so the app company is caught if it demands or receives the fee. The duty to offer a free method applies to the provider or agent [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The documents don't address the app company's legal relationship with the agent, so I can't say whether the agent is responsible for the app's fee.

## What you can do or ask

- **Ask in writing** what costs apply to each payment method before you agree to use the card option [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Ask for the fee-free method.** The provider must permit at least one fee-free payment method (other than your own bank fees) and must allow Centrepay or another electronic funds transfer [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). Electronic funds transfer is the prescribed payment method [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **Ask for receipts.** You're entitled to a written receipt for rent. If you pay other than in person, you can request it at the time of payment, and it must be given within 5 business days [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **More information:** The standard tenancy form directs renters to consumer.vic.gov.au/renting [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

## What the documents don't cover

- Whether a slower bank transfer is an acceptable substitute. The law requires a free method to be "reasonably available," but the documents don't say whether delay is relevant.
- A specific complaint process for an unlawful app fee, beyond the general resources above.
- Whether a particular app's fee is a "payment surcharge fee permitted under any other Act."

This is general information, not legal advice. For a specific dispute, check with Consumer Affairs Victoria.

All three points are covered: the answer states that 'A no-additional-cost payment method must be reasonably available to you... other than for bank fees or account fees'; on the hardest point it says 'A person, other than an ADI, must not demand or receive a fee... in relation to the payment of rent' with the 'payment surcharge fees permitted under any other Act' exception, and 'Whether the fee goes to the app or the agent doesn't change that, because the main prohibition applies to "a person"'; and it gives next steps including 'Ask for the fee-free method' and 'check with Consumer Affairs Victoria'.

question: My lease has a pet clause saying I must have the carpets professionally cleaned when I leave. I cleaned them myself and they're back to how they were when I moved in, but the agent wants a receipt from a professional cleaner. Do I have to pay for one, and what would help show the carpets' condition?
answer:
**Short answer:** Probably not, if the carpets are already restored to their pre-tenancy condition. The Act and Regulations only require professional cleaning when it is actually needed to restore the premises. The documents don't say that a receipt from a professional cleaner is required.

**What the law says**

- Your lease term can only require professional cleaning if it is in the standard form. A term requiring professional cleaning at the end of the tenancy is a prohibited term unless it is in the standard form [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- The standard-form term applies only if professional cleaning "becomes required to restore the premises to the condition they were in immediately before the start of the tenancy, taking into account fair wear and tear" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- The Regulations go further. The provider "must not require the renter to arrange professional cleaning or cleaning to a professional standard at the end of the tenancy" unless either (a) professional cleaning was carried out before the tenancy and the renter was told so, or (b) professional cleaning "is required to restore the rented premises to the same condition they were in immediately before the start of the tenancy, having regard to the condition report and taking into account fair wear and tear" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- At the end of the agreement, you must leave the premises "as far as practicable" reasonably clean and in the same condition as when you moved in, allowing for fair wear and tear [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- The provider can claim from the bond the reasonable cost of cleaning only if the premises were not left reasonably clean, "having regard to the condition of the premises at the commencement of the residential rental agreement" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

**What you can do or ask**

1. **Check your move-in condition report.** The provider must give you a condition report before you move in [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). A condition report signed by both parties is conclusive evidence of the state of repair or general condition on the day specified in it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). If it describes the carpets, it is the key comparison point under the Regulations [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
2. **Ask whether professional cleaning is actually required.** Under the Regulations, the test is whether professional cleaning is required to restore the premises, having regard to the condition report [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). If you have restored the carpets to their move-in state, you can say so in writing and ask the agent to identify what remains that needs professional cleaning.
3. **Ask whether the carpets were professionally cleaned before you moved in.** If they were, and you were told so, the Regulations allow the provider to require professional cleaning [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). Your condition report or the agent's records may show this.
4. **Check the bond claim if one is made.** Before a bond claim for the provider is made, the provider must give you "bond claim evidence" that supports it, and that evidence "must not conflict with a statement in a condition report" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). You can dispute the claim within 14 days by giving the Bond Authority written notice that the claim is subject to a Tribunal application [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
5. **Keep your own evidence.** The documents don't specifically list photos or receipts as evidence. However, your cleaning records, dated photos, and any comments you make on the condition report would help show the condition of the carpets. A condition report comment disagreeing with a statement is relevant under the Act [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

**What the documents don't cover**

- Whether your lease's pet clause is in the standard form. You should check this, because a non-standard professional-cleaning term is prohibited and void [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- Whether a receipt from a professional cleaner is ever required. The documents don't say that.
- Whether photos or receipts would be accepted as evidence of carpet condition, beyond the condition report.
- Whether the carpets were professionally cleaned before you moved in.

This is general information based on the retrieved documents, not legal advice. If the agent insists on a professional clean, you can seek advice from Consumer Affairs Victoria or apply to the Victorian Civil and Administrative Tribunal.

**Sources and versions**

- [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, version 115 (in force from 13 October 2026, per file metadata).
- [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf) *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*, version 009 (in force from 30 June 2026, per file metadata). The Regulations contain the professional cleaning term at regulation 12 and in Form 1 (clause 11).

Reg 12 is covered by the (a)/(b) exceptions. question: When I moved out I agreed the agent could take an amount for cleaning out of my bond. Then my full bond came back to me, and now the agent has sent a separate invoice for the cleaning. Do I have to pay it? Is agreeing to a bond deduction the same as agreeing to pay an invoice?
answer:
**Short answer:** The documents don't say whether agreeing to a bond deduction also means agreeing to pay a separate invoice. They do set out when a landlord or agent can claim cleaning costs, and what they must show.

## What the law says

- **Bond claims for cleaning:** A rental provider can claim from the bond for "the reasonable cost of cleaning any part of the premises, if the premises were not left reasonably clean by the renter, having regard to the condition of the premises at the commencement of the residential rental agreement" [1, s 411AB(1)(c)].
- **Evidence before a claim:** Before a claim for repayment to the provider is made, the provider or agent "must give each renter bond claim evidence that supports the claim," at least 3 days before, and that evidence "must not conflict with a statement in a condition report" [1, s 411(1A) and (1B)].
- **Professional cleaning:** The standard term allows the renter to be required to pay for professional cleaning only "if professional cleaning becomes required to restore the premises to the condition they were in immediately before the start of the tenancy, having regard to the condition report and taking into account fair wear and tear" [2, Sch. 1 Form 1, item 11; reg 12(2)]. A term requiring the renter to pay for professional cleaning is prohibited unless it is in the standard form [1, s 27B(1)(e)].
- **End-of-tenancy inspection:** The provider or agent must complete the final inspection and fill in the condition report "within 10 days after the end date of the agreement," give the renter an opportunity to attend if possible, and "allow for fair wear and tear" [2, Sch. 1 Form 4, item 6].

## What the documents don't cover

- Whether agreeing to a bond deduction waives your rights or makes you liable for further amounts.
- Whether an agent can invoice you separately for cleaning after the bond has been refunded in full.
- How a separate invoice should be issued or disputed.

## What you can do or ask

1. **Ask for the condition report** from the start of the tenancy and compare it with the end-of-tenancy report. Cleaning costs are assessed against the condition at the start [1, s 411AB(1)(c)], and the report is the key reference [2, Form 4].
2. **Ask for the evidence** behind the cleaning charge. For bond claims, the provider must give bond claim evidence [1, s 411(1A)]. The documents don't say whether this applies to a separate invoice, but you can still ask.
3. **Check whether a professional cleaning term applies.** Ask whether the premises were professionally cleaned before you moved in and whether you were told so [2, reg 12(1)(a)]. Check your agreement for any cleaning term.
4. **Check fair wear and tear.** Cleaning needed only because of normal wear does not fall on you under the standard terms [2, Form 1, item 11].
5. **Seek further advice.** Consumer Affairs Victoria's renting information is at consumer.vic.gov.au/renting [2, Sch. 1 Form 1]. The documents don't set out a process for disputing an invoice. If the agreement contains a harsh or unconscionable term, you may apply to the Tribunal [1, s 28].

**Documents used:**
- [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version **No. 115** (in force from 13 October 2026, the most recent version retrieved and in force today).
- [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf) Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version **No. 009** (in force from 30 June 2026).

This is general information from the retrieved documents, not legal advice. For a decision on your specific invoice, speak with Consumer Affairs Victoria or a tenancy lawyer.

question: A tap broke and I had to turn off the water to the whole house. The emergency repair contact says the owner only lets their own tradespeople do repairs, and none of them can come yet. Do I have to wait, or can I get it fixed myself?
answer:
**Short answer:** Based on the documents, you don't have to wait indefinitely. A burst water service is an urgent repair, and in some circumstances you can arrange the repair yourself and seek reimbursement. The documents don't settle whether an owner can restrict repairs to their own tradespeople, so you may need to take that further.

**What the law says**

- The governing documents are the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* (version 115, in force from 13 October 2026 per its metadata) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) and the *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021* (Authorised Version No. 009, as at 30 June 2026) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- A "burst water service" is an urgent repair, and so is a "failure or breakdown of the gas, electricity or water supply to rented premises" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- The rental provider must carry out urgent repairs after being notified [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- Only a suitably qualified person may do repairs, both urgent and non-urgent [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). A "suitably qualified person" includes a registered or licensed tradesperson where the work requires it [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- Agreements cannot exclude or restrict the rights in the Act [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

**What you can do or ask**

1. **Notify in writing.** Renters must give written notice to the provider as soon as practicable after becoming aware of damage or a breakdown [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Use the emergency contact details in your agreement [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
2. **Ask for immediate repair.** You may arrange urgent repairs if you have taken reasonable steps to get the provider or their agent to carry out the repairs immediately, and you are unable to get them to do so [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The documents don't define "reasonable steps" or set a waiting period, so keep a written record of every request and their response.
3. **Get the repair done properly.** The repairer must be a suitably qualified person [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
4. **Give written notice of cost.** You must give the provider 7 days' written notice of the repairs and their cost [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
5. **Claim reimbursement.** The provider must reimburse the reasonable cost within 7 days of receiving your written notice. The liability is capped at the reasonable cost or a prescribed amount, whichever is less [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The regulations summary states the renter may be reimbursed directly for the reasonable cost up to $2,500 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
6. **Go to VCAT if needed.** You can apply to VCAT for an order requiring the provider to carry out urgent repairs if you cannot meet the cost, the cost is more than $2,500, or the provider refuses to pay you back [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). VCAT must hear an urgent repair application within 2 business days [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). If the provider doesn't reimburse you within 7 days of your written notice, you can apply for a compensation or compliance order [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

**What the documents don't cover**

- Whether an owner can lawfully insist that only their own tradespeople carry out repairs. The documents only say that agreement terms cannot restrict Act rights [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- How long a renter must wait before "reasonable steps" are met.
- Whether your specific tap failure falls within the urgent repair definition beyond the categories listed above.

This is general information from the retrieved documents, not legal advice. If the owner refuses, Consumer Affairs Victoria or VCAT can advise on your specific circumstances.

question: I signed a lease and picked up the keys, but before moving in I found damp, mould and rotting timber in the house. What are my options? Can I cancel, ask for repairs, or ask for lower rent?
answer:
**Short answer:** Under the law in the documents, you can't simply cancel because of the damp, mould and rotting timber, but you can require repairs and, in some cases, go to VCAT. The documents don't clearly give you a right to a rent reduction, and I could not confirm the cancellation rules from the retrieved text.

I'm relying on the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, Authorised Version No. 115, incorporating amendments as at 13 October 2026 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf), and the *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*, S.R. No. 3/2021, version 009 (in force 30 June 2026) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). These are the current versions as of today (5 November 2026).

---

## What the law says

- **Mould and damp:** Each room must be free from "mould and damp caused by or related to the building structure" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). The premises must also be "structurally sound and weatherproof" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **Landlord's obligations:** The rental provider must ensure the premises comply with the rental minimum standards and are "vacant and reasonably clean when the renter moves in," and must maintain them "in good repair and in a fit condition for occupation" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **Urgent repairs:** The Act defines urgent repairs to include "any fault or damage that makes rented premises... unsafe or insecure," including "the presence of mould or damp caused by or related to the building structure" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Whether rotting timber is "unsafe or insecure" is a factual question. The documents don't say.

## Your options

**1. Record the problems in writing now.**
- Renters must give written notice "as soon as practicable after becoming aware of" damage or breakdowns [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- Fill in the condition report within 5 business days after moving in, note anything that needs repair, and take dated photos [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- If you disagree with the condition report, you may apply to VCAT to correct it within 30 days after the start date of the agreement [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

**2. Ask for non-urgent repairs.**
- If the landlord doesn't carry out repairs within 14 days after written notice, you can apply to the Director (Consumer Affairs) to investigate [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- You can also apply to VCAT for an order requiring repairs if they aren't done within 14 days of notice. VCAT must hear that application within 7 days [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- VCAT can order specified repairs, use of a suitably qualified person, and compensation [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

**3. Arrange urgent repairs yourself, if they qualify.**
- You may arrange urgent repairs if you have taken reasonable steps to get the landlord to do them immediately and they haven't [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- The landlord must reimburse the reasonable cost within 7 days of written notice of the repairs and cost, up to $2500 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). You must give 7 days' written notice of the repairs and cost first [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

question: Our rental was broken into several times while we were moving out, and the lease hasn't ended yet. The burglars damaged the plumbing and wiring, so we can't even clean properly. What are our options before the lease ends?
answer:
**Short answer:** Notify your landlord or agent in writing now, and ask them to carry out urgent repairs. If they don't, you may be able to arrange urgent repairs yourself and seek reimbursement. Cleaning is a separate issue that mostly arises at the end of the lease. The retrieved documents don't cover insurance or police reporting.

Sources: [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) is the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, Authorised Version No. 115, as at 13 October 2026. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf) is the *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021* (S.R. No. 3/2021), metadata version 009, in force from 30 June 2026.

## What the law says

- **Damage and reporting:** You must give the landlord written notice "as soon as practicable" after becoming aware of damage or a breakdown of facilities [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The notice must state that the damage occurred and its nature [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Who is liable:** You must not intentionally or negligently damage the premises, and fair wear and tear doesn't count [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Burglars aren't obviously your "visitors," since a visitor is someone on the premises with your permission [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Whether you're liable depends on the facts, and the documents don't resolve that.
- **Urgent repairs:** The definition includes a burst water service, a blocked or broken lavatory system, a failure of the water or electricity supply, a dangerous electrical fault, and any fault or damage that makes the premises unsafe or insecure [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Your situation may fall within several of these.
- **Landlord's duty:** The landlord must carry out urgent repairs after being notified [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). Only a suitably qualified person may do repairs [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **Cleaning:** While you live there, you must keep the premises reasonably clean [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). At the end, you must leave them as far as practicable reasonably clean and in the same condition as when you moved in, allowing for fair wear and tear [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The landlord can't require professional cleaning unless it's needed to restore the condition from the start of the tenancy, having regard to the condition report [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

## What you can do or ask

1. **Give written notice now.** Describe the break-in and the damage to the plumbing and wiring, and ask for urgent repairs. Keep a copy and any proof of sending. Electronic notice is allowed [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
2. **Arrange urgent repairs if the landlord doesn't act.** You may do so if you've taken reasonable steps to get the landlord to repair immediately and you can't [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). You must give the landlord 7 days' written notice of the repairs and the cost [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The landlord must reimburse the reasonable cost within 7 days of that notice, and the regulations say reimbursement is capped at $2,500 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
3. **Apply to VCAT if needed.** You can apply for an order requiring urgent repairs if you can't meet the cost, the cost is more than the prescribed amount, or the landlord refuses to pay you back [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). VCAT must hear the application within 2 business days [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
4. **Ask for a lock change if needed.** You must get consent to change a master-key lock, and the landlord must not unreasonably refuse [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). If consent is withheld and you believe that's unreasonable, you can apply to VCAT [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
5. **Consider rent into the Rent Special Account.** After giving notice requiring repairs, you can apply to VCAT to pay rent into the Rent Special Account if the landlord fails to do the repairs [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The landlord can avoid this only by showing financial hardship [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
6. **Document everything.** Take dated, labelled photos of the damage and the condition of the premises [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

## Risks to watch

- The landlord could give you a repair notice if they believe you caused the damage by failing to take care [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). You would then have 14 days to repair it, or the landlord may repair it and charge you [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- The landlord can claim from your bond for reasonable repair or cleaning costs for damage you caused, or for cleaning if the premises weren't left reasonably clean [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

## What the documents don't cover

- Whether a burglary counts as your responsibility, beyond the general rule above.
- Insurance claims, police reports, or whether the landlord's insurer covers the damage.
- The specific criteria for ending the lease early if the premises become unfit to live in. The regulations mention this under s 91ZD of the Act [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf), but I didn't retrieve that section's text.

This is general information based on the retrieved documents, not legal advice. For your specific situation, contact Consumer Affairs Victoria or a community legal centre.

question: My rent app charges a fee when I pay by card. There's also a manual bank transfer option with no fee, but it's slower. Can the app charge me the card fee? Does it matter whether the fee goes to the app company or to the agent?
answer:
**Short answer:** Probably not, if the app is charging you a fee to pay rent. Victorian law prohibits charging a rent payment fee, with an exception for surcharges permitted under another Act, and the retrieved documents do not identify any such Act. Whether the fee goes to the app company or the agent doesn't change this, because the prohibition applies to "a person."

**What the law says**

- **Fees for paying rent are prohibited.** From 31 March 2026, the regulations list "rent payment (other than payment surcharge fees permitted under any other Act)" as a prohibited application and rent payment fee [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). The Act says a person other than an ADI must not demand or receive a fee for a prescribed matter in relation to the payment of rent [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). An ADI is an authorised deposit-taking institution, such as a bank.
- **The app company is covered.** The prohibition applies to "a person," not only to the rental provider or agent [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). So the question of who receives the fee doesn't remove the prohibition.
- **The provider or agent must offer a free method.** The provider or agent must ensure that a payment method incurring no additional costs (other than bank or account fees on the renter's bank account) is reasonably available to the renter. The penalty is 80 penalty units for a natural person or 400 for a body corporate [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Bank transfer must be allowed.** The provider or agent must permit payment by Centrepay and by any prescribed payment method [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The prescribed method is electronic funds transfer [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). Your manual bank transfer option fits this category.
- **Costs must be disclosed.** Before you agree to a payment method, the provider or agent must tell you about any costs you may incur, including third-party transaction fees [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

**What you can do or ask**

1. Ask the agent or provider in writing whether the card fee is a payment surcharge permitted under another Act, and which Act. The documents I retrieved don't identify one.
2. Ask them to confirm that the fee-free bank transfer method is available to you. Under the law, the slower speed of that method doesn't make it any less available.
3. If they insist on the card fee, you can point to the prohibition in the Act and regulations and the disclosure requirement above.

**Version and gaps**

- Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 115, in force from 13 October 2026 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The regulations are Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version No. 009, in force from 30 June 2026 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). Both are the current versions as of today.
- The documents don't say how a renter should complain about or enforce these rules, so I can't advise on that process.
- The documents don't cover whether your specific app is an ADI. If it is, the fee prohibition in s 51A doesn't apply to it.

question: My lease has a pet clause saying I must have the carpets professionally cleaned when I leave. I cleaned them myself and they're back to how they were when I moved in, but the agent wants a receipt from a professional cleaner. Do I have to pay for one, and what would help show the carpets' condition?
answer:
**Short answer:** Probably not, if the carpets are already back to their move-in condition. The law only requires professional cleaning when it is *required* to restore the premises, and the documents don't say whether a self-clean can meet that standard.

**Documents used:** *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, version 115 (file dated 13 October 2026) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf), and *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*, version 009 (file dated 30 June 2026) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). Both are the versions in force today.

## What the law says

- **The clause is limited.** A term requiring professional cleaning at the end of a tenancy is prohibited unless it is in the standard form [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Under the Regulations, the provider must not require professional cleaning at the end of the tenancy unless it was carried out before the tenancy started and you were told so, or it "is required to restore the rented premises to the same condition they were in immediately before the start of the tenancy, having regard to the condition report and taking into account fair wear and tear" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **You pay only if cleaning becomes required.** The standard-form term says the renter must have the premises professionally cleaned, or pay for it, "if professional cleaning becomes required to restore the premises" to their starting condition, again taking fair wear and tear into account [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **Your general duty.** At the end of the agreement you must leave the premises "as far as practicable" reasonably clean, and in the same condition as when you moved in, allowing for fair wear and tear [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Bond deductions.** The provider can claim the reasonable cost of cleaning only "if the premises were not left reasonably clean by the renter, having regard to the condition of the premises at the commencement" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

## What you can do or ask

1. **Ask the agent what makes professional cleaning "required".** Under the law, the question is whether it is needed to restore the carpets to their move-in condition, not whether the clause mentions it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
2. **Gather evidence of the carpets' condition.** The move-in condition report is key. Your signed copy is evidence of the premises' state, and a statement in a report signed by both parties is conclusive evidence of the state of repair or general condition on the day specified [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The prescribed form says to keep the report safe and take dated, labelled photos at the start and end of the tenancy [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
3. **Check the end-of-tenancy report.** The provider must complete it within 10 days after the agreement ends, give you the chance to attend if possible, and allow for fair wear and tear [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). You can record disagreement on the copy you keep [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
4. **Check any bond claim.** Before claiming bond for a reason, the provider must give you bond claim evidence at least 3 days before the claim [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). That evidence must not conflict with a statement in the condition report [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
5. **Use the dispute process if needed.** If the provider claims the bond, you can be notified and have 14 days to tell the Authority that the claim is subject to a Tribunal application [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

## What the documents don't cover

- **Receipts:** Nothing in the documents says you must provide a receipt from a professional cleaner. The agent's request may be reasonable as evidence, but the documents don't require it.
- **Whether a DIY clean is enough:** The documents don't define "required" or say how to prove carpets are restored. That depends on the facts, such as the move-in report, your photos, and the carpets' condition.
- **The pet clause:** The Regulations' pet provision deals only with seeking consent to keep a pet [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). Nothing I retrieved links pets to cleaning obligations, so the cleaning term's legal basis is the professional-cleaning provisions above.

This is general information based on the retrieved documents, not legal advice. If the agent refuses to return your bond or the dispute continues, Consumer Affairs Victoria or VCAT can advise on your specific lease.

The documents don't say whether agreeing to a bond deduction is the same as agreeing to pay a separate invoice, or whether a full bond refund ends the agent's right to claim more. ## What you can do or ask

3. **Check whether the charge is reasonable.** Only a "reasonable cost" of cleaning is recoverable, and only for cleaning needed because the premises were not left reasonably clean [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). If the cleaning was professional, check whether the Regulations allow it [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

5. **Know the Tribunal route.** Any person with an interest in a bond claim can apply to the Tribunal for a bond repayment order [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). If you want a firm answer on your situation, consider getting advice from Consumer Affairs Victoria or a tenancy legal service, since these documents don't settle those questions.

question: A tap broke and I had to turn off the water to the whole house. The emergency repair contact says the owner only lets their own tradespeople do repairs, and none of them can come yet. Do I have to wait, or can I get it fixed myself?
answer:
**Short answer:** You don't have to wait for the owner's tradespeople. Under the Act, if you have taken reasonable steps to get the owner to repair the tap immediately and they haven't, you may arrange the repair yourself and seek reimbursement. Whether a broken tap qualifies as an urgent repair depends on the facts.

**What the law says**

- **Source:** The Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version **No. 115**, in force from 13 October 2026, is the version that applies today [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Your right to arrange urgent repairs:** You may arrange urgent repairs if (a) you have taken reasonable steps to get the owner or their agent to carry out the repairs immediately, and (b) you are unable to get them to do so [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Urgent repairs:** The Act defines urgent repairs to include work to repair a burst water service, and a failure or breakdown of an essential water service or of an appliance or fitting that uses or supplies water and is malfunctioning in a way that wastes a substantial amount of water [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). A tap that is leaking or has cut off supply to the house will likely fall within these categories, but the Act does not name taps specifically, so it may be disputed.
- **Who can do the work:** The Act defines a "suitably qualified person" to include a tradesperson who is registered or licensed for the relevant work, where that work requires registration or a licence [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Cost limit:** The owner must reimburse the reasonable cost of the repairs, capped at the reasonable cost or the prescribed amount, whichever is less [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The Act refers to a "prescribed amount" but the excerpts I retrieved do not state its figure. The only $2,500 figure in the retrieved material appears in the rooming house form of the Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 (Authorised Version reference: S.R. No. 3/2021, version 009) and does not clearly apply to your situation [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

**What you can do or ask**

1. **Notify the owner in writing now.** You must give written notice of the breakdown as soon as practicable [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The rental agreement form also says that for an urgent repair the renter should notify the rental provider in writing, and it includes an emergency contact section [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). Keep a copy of your message and note the time you sent it.
2. **Keep a record of your attempts.** Document each time you asked the owner or agent to act immediately and their response. This supports the "reasonable steps" requirement [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
3. **Get the repair done by a qualified person.** Use a registered or licensed tradesperson where the work requires it [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
4. **Give written notice of the repair and its cost.** You must give the owner 7 days' written notice of the repairs carried out and their cost [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Keep receipts.
5. **Claim reimbursement.** The owner must reimburse the reasonable cost within 7 days after receiving your written notice of the repairs and cost [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
6. **If the owner refuses to pay or the cost is high, apply to VCAT.** You can apply to the Victorian Civil and Administrative Tribunal for an order requiring the owner to carry out urgent repairs if you cannot meet the cost, the cost exceeds the prescribed amount, or the owner refuses to pay for your repairs [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The Tribunal must hear the application within 2 business days after it is made [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

**What the documents don't cover**

- The retrieved documents do not say whether an owner can insist on using only its own tradespeople. They also do not say whether the owner's refusal to send anyone else, combined with the lack of availability, counts as being "unable to get" the repair. That will depend on the facts, and VCAT would decide disputed cases.
- The retrieved documents do not state the prescribed amount for residential rental urgent repairs.

If the water remains off, it may also be worth contacting Consumer Affairs Victoria for guidance on your specific circumstances.

question: I signed a lease and picked up the keys, but before moving in I found damp, mould and rotting timber in the house. What are my options? Can I cancel, ask for repairs, or ask for lower rent?
answer:
## What the law says

**Minimum standards.** The Regulations require that the rented premises be "structurally sound and weatherproof" and that "each room in the rented premises must be free from mould and damp caused by or related to the building structure" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). The documents don't mention rotting timber by name, but it may fall under the structural soundness standard [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

**Landlord's duties at move-in.** The rental provider "must ensure that the premises comply with the rental minimum standards, and is vacant and reasonably clean when the renter moves in," and must "maintain the premises in good repair" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

**Condition report.** Before you move in, the provider must give you "2 copies of a condition report" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). You must return a copy within "5 business days after entering into occupation" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). If the report you sign is also signed by the provider, it is conclusive evidence of the condition on that day [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). A condition report given to the provider is also notice of any defects it states [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). You can apply to VCAT to amend an inaccurate or incomplete report within 30 days after the agreement commenced [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

**Urgent repairs.** The Act defines urgent repairs to include "a failure to comply with any rental minimum standards" and "any fault or damage that makes rented premises... unsafe or insecure, including... the presence of mould or damp caused by or related to the building structure" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Whether your mould or damp is "unsafe or insecure" is a question of fact the documents don't resolve.

---

## Your options

**1. Cancel the lease (possibly).**
Under the Act, a lease "does not terminate and must not be terminated except in accordance with this Division or Part 7 or 8" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The relevant route is s 91L: a lease terminates if the renter "has not entered into possession of the rented premises and has given a notice of termination" on the ground that the premises are "not in good repair," "unfit for human habitation," or "do not meet any rental minimum standards" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). This is only available if you have not yet entered possession. The documents do not define "entered into possession," so you should confirm whether picking up the keys and inspecting counts, and get advice before relying on this route.

**2. Ask for repairs.**
- **Give written notice now.** You must give written notice "as soon as practicable after becoming aware of" damage [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The Regulations also say the renter must notify the provider in writing of damage as soon as practicable [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). Record the defects in the condition report and take photos [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **Urgent repairs.** If the problem is urgent, you may arrange repairs if you have "taken reasonable steps" to get the provider to act immediately and the provider cannot be reached or does not act [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). You must give "7 days written notice of the repairs carried out and the cost," and the provider must reimburse the reasonable cost within 7 days, whichever is less [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The Regulations say reimbursement is for repairs "up to $2500" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). Repairs must be done by a suitably qualified person [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **Non-urgent repairs.** If the provider does not carry out repairs within 14 days of written notice, you can apply to the Director under s 74 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf), or to VCAT under s 75, which must be heard "within 7 days" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The Regulations also say you may apply to VCAT if repairs are not done "within 14 days of receiving notice" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **Urgent repair applications.** You can apply to VCAT for an order requiring urgent repairs if you cannot meet the cost, the cost exceeds $2500, or the provider refuses to pay for repairs you arrange [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). VCAT must hear such applications "within 2 business days" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Rent into the Rent Special Account.** If you have given notice requiring repairs, you may apply to VCAT to pay rent into the Rent Special Account, which the Tribunal must authorise if the provider has failed to repair and cannot show financial hardship [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). This is a way to put pressure on the provider; it does not reduce the rent.

**3. Ask for lower rent.**
The documents do not contain a provision that lets you reduce rent because of defects. The only rent-related hardship power I found (s 91U) allows VCAT to reduce the term of a fixed-term agreement or terminate it, and only where there has been "an unforeseen change in the applicant's circumstances" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). It does not reduce rent. The documents therefore do not answer whether you can get a rent reduction for these defects. You would need to check other sources, such as Consumer Affairs Victoria, or seek advice.

---

## Documents relied on

- **Residential Tenancies Act 1997**, version 115, in force from 13 October 2026 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). This is the version in force today.
- **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021** (S.R. No. 3/2021), version 009, in force from 30 June 2026 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

This is general information, not legal advice. Given the timing of your move-in and the notice requirements, consider contacting Consumer Affairs Victoria or Victoria Legal Aid promptly.

(3) It describes the repair route: urgent repairs include 'a failure to comply with any rental minimum standards', and it also covers the good-repair duty and the non-urgent repair process.

question: Our rental was broken into several times while we were moving out, and the lease hasn't ended yet. The burglars damaged the plumbing and wiring, so we can't even clean properly. What are our options before the lease ends?
answer:
**Short answer:** Under the Act, the damage is the landlord's responsibility to repair if it is an urgent repair, and you can arrange urgent repairs yourself in some circumstances. You must report the damage in writing now.

Sources: *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, Authorised Version No. 115, incorporating amendments as at 13 October 2026 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf), and *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021* (S.R. No. 3/2021, file version v009, dated 30 June 2026) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). These are the versions in force today.

## What the law says

- **Urgent repairs include the damage you describe.** "Urgent repairs" covers a burst water service, a blocked or broken lavatory system, a dangerous electrical fault, and "any fault or damage that makes rented premises... unsafe or insecure" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Your plumbing and wiring damage fits these categories, and damage that leaves the home insecure after break-ins may too.
- **You must report the damage in writing.** A renter must give written notice "as soon as practicable" after becoming aware of damage [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) (s 72AA). The notice must state the fact that the damage occurred and its nature [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) (s 62).
- **Your own damage duty.** A renter and any visitor must not intentionally or negligently damage the premises [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) (s 61). A "visitor" is someone on the premises with the renter's permission [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The documents do not say how damage from people who broke in without permission is treated, so this needs advice from a specialist body.
- **Cleaning at the end.** A renter must keep the premises reasonably clean [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) (s 63(1)). At the end of the agreement, you must leave them "as far as practicable" reasonably clean [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) (s 63(2)). The landlord cannot require professional cleaning unless it is needed to restore the premises to their condition at the start of the tenancy, taking fair wear and tear into account [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

## What you can do or ask

1. **Report in writing now.** Tell the landlord or agent in writing about the break-in and each damaged item. Include the plumbing and wiring.
2. **Ask for urgent repairs.** The landlord must carry out urgent repairs after being notified [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). Name the urgent repairs you need.
3. **Arrange urgent repairs yourself if the landlord does not act.** You may do this if you have taken reasonable steps to get the landlord to repair immediately, and the landlord cannot or does not do it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) (s 72(1)). Before doing so:
   - Only a suitably qualified person may do repairs [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
   - You must give the landlord 7 days' written notice of the repairs and their cost [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) (s 72(2)(a)).
   - The landlord must reimburse the reasonable cost within 7 days after receiving written notice of the repairs and cost [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) (s 72(2)(c)). The reimbursement is capped at the reasonable cost or the prescribed amount, whichever is less [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The regulations state the prescribed reimbursement is "up to $2500" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
4. **Apply to VCAT if needed.** You may apply to VCAT for an order requiring urgent repairs if you cannot meet the cost, the cost is more than $2500, or the landlord refuses to pay for repairs you carry out [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). VCAT must hear the application within 2 business days [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) (s 73(2)).
5. **Non-urgent repairs (if any remain).** If you give written notice and the landlord does not carry out the repairs within 14 days, you can apply to the Director or to VCAT [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) (ss 74–75).
6. **Rent into the Rent Special Account.** If you have given notice requiring repairs, you may apply to VCAT to pay rent into the Rent Special Account [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) (s 77).
7. **Locks.** The regulations require the landlord to provide locks on all windows capable of having one and deadlocks on external doors that can be secured [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). Given the break-ins, ask for these to be checked and fixed. The Act also allows a renter to apply to VCAT to change a lock without consent if the Tribunal finds consent is not required [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) (s 71).

## What the documents do not cover

- Whether the landlord's insurance pays for the break-in damage.
- Police reporting or any criminal-injury process.
- How a bond claim would treat damage caused by burglars, beyond the general rule that a landlord may claim for damage "caused by the renter or a renter's visitor" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) (s 411AB(1)(a)).

For advice on these points, contact Consumer Affairs Victoria or VCAT, or get legal advice.

question: My rent app charges a fee when I pay by card. There's also a manual bank transfer option with no fee, but it's slower. Can the app charge me the card fee? Does it matter whether the fee goes to the app company or to the agent?
answer:
**Short answer:** Probably not. Victorian law generally prohibits a rent payment fee, and the prohibition covers any person who charges it, not just the agent. The documents I found don't say whether any "payment surcharge" is permitted under another Act, so check that before accepting the fee.

**What the law says**

- **Fee prohibition:** A person other than an ADI must not demand or receive a fee for any prescribed matter in relation to the payment of rent [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The Regulations list "rent payment (other than payment surcharge fees permitted under any other Act)" as a prescribed matter, effective from 31 March 2026 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). The exception applies only to surcharges permitted under another Act, and the documents don't identify any such Act.

question: My lease has a pet clause saying I must have the carpets professionally cleaned when I leave. I cleaned them myself and they're back to how they were when I moved in, but the agent wants a receipt from a professional cleaner. Do I have to pay for one, and what would help show the carpets' condition?
answer:
**Short answer:** Based on the documents, you probably don't have to pay for a professional clean if the carpets are back to their move-in condition. However, the documents don't show your lease terms or whether the carpets were professionally cleaned before you moved in, so this depends on facts I can't confirm.

*Current law: Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version 115 (in force from 13 October 2026), and Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version 009 (in force from 30 June 2026).*

## What the law says

- **The Act limits when cleaning terms are allowed.** A lease can include a professional-cleaning term only if it is in the standard form and professional cleaning becomes required to restore the premises to their starting condition, taking fair wear and tear into account [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). A term requiring professional cleaning at the end of the tenancy is prohibited unless it is in the standard form [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **The Regulations set the test.** The provider must not require professional cleaning at the end of the tenancy unless either (a) professional cleaning was done before you moved in and you were told so, or (b) professional cleaning is required to restore the premises to the condition they were in before the tenancy started, having regard to the condition report and fair wear and tear [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **The basic duty is "reasonably clean."** At the end of the agreement, you must leave the premises as far as practicable reasonably clean, and in the same condition as when you moved in, allowing for fair wear and tear [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Bond claims for cleaning are limited.** A provider can claim the reasonable cost of cleaning only if the premises were not left reasonably clean, having regard to their condition at the start [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

## What this means for you

If your carpets are back to their move-in condition, professional cleaning is arguably not "required" under the test above. Whether the clause is enforceable also depends on whether the term is in the standard form, which the documents don't show. The Act also says a term can be declared invalid if it is harsh or unconscionable, and the Tribunal can make that call [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

The documents don't say that an agent can insist on a receipt from a professional cleaner, or whether a self-clean receipt is enough.

## What helps show the carpets' condition

- **Your condition report.** The start-of-tenancy report is important. A signed report is conclusive evidence of the state of repair or general condition on the day specified in it [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The Regulations say the report helps resolve disputes over cleaning [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **Photos.** The form says to take photos at the beginning and end of the tenancy, dated, labelled by room, and attached to the report [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). Photos are useful in a dispute about condition [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **The end-of-tenancy inspection.** The provider must complete the final inspection and the end-of-tenancy part of the condition report within 10 days after the agreement ends, and give you a chance to attend if possible [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Attend if you can, and note any disagreement in writing.
- **Your own comments.** You can record disagreement with any statement on your copy of the report [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

The documents don't mention cleaning receipts, so a self-clean receipt isn't addressed.

## What you can ask or do

1. **Ask the agent in writing** which lease term requires professional cleaning, and whether the carpets were professionally cleaned before you moved in and whether you were told so [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
2. **Ask for the condition report** and compare it with your photos.
3. **Attend or request the end-of-tenancy inspection**.
4. **If the bond is claimed for cleaning,** the provider must give you bond claim evidence at least 3 days before claiming, and that evidence must not conflict with the condition report [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
5. **If there's a dispute,** the documents mention VCAT for harsh or unconscionable terms [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf), but they don't set out the full dispute process. Consumer Affairs Victoria can give you guidance, but I haven't checked that source.

answer:
**Short answer:** The documents don't say whether agreeing to a bond deduction also means agreeing to pay a separate invoice. Based on the statute, though, a cleaning cost is a bond claim item, and the bond has already been returned to you. You shouldn't pay the invoice just because you agreed to a deduction. Ask for the evidence and check it first.

Today's law is the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, Authorised Version No. 115, which incorporates amendments as at 13 October 2026 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). ---

- **Cleaning is a bond item.** A provider may claim from the bond the reasonable cost of cleaning any part of the premises if they were not left reasonably clean by the renter, compared with their condition at the start of the tenancy [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Your duty.** At the end of the agreement, a renter must leave the premises, as far as practicable, reasonably clean and in the same condition as when they moved in, allowing for fair wear and tear [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Evidence is required.** At least 3 days before a claim for repayment to the provider is made, the provider must give each renter "bond claim evidence" supporting the claim. That evidence must not conflict with the condition report [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Professional cleaning limits.** The provider must not require you to arrange professional cleaning unless the rental premises were professionally cleaned before you moved in and you were told so, or professional cleaning is needed to restore the premises to their starting condition, taking fair wear and tear into account [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). Terms requiring professional cleaning at the end of a tenancy are prohibited unless they are in the standard form [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **A refund doesn't end all claims.** A person who has recovered compensation from a bond is not barred from taking proceedings to recover an additional amount [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). - Whether an agent can issue a separate invoice after the bond has been refunded, and how such a debt would be enforced.
- The time limit for a provider to pursue cleaning costs after a full refund.

question: A tap broke and I had to turn off the water to the whole house. The emergency repair contact says the owner only lets their own tradespeople do repairs, and none of them can come yet. Do I have to wait, or can I get it fixed myself?
answer:
**Short answer:** You don't have to simply wait. Under the Act, if the owner can't get the repair done promptly, you may arrange it yourself and seek reimbursement, provided you follow the required steps. The documents don't address whether the owner can restrict repairs to their own tradespeople, so that point needs separate advice.

**What the law says**

- **Urgent repairs:** "Urgent repairs" include work to repair "a burst water service" and "a failure or breakdown of the gas, electricity or water supply to rented premises" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). A whole-house water shut-off likely falls within this, though the documents don't address a broken tap specifically.
- **Your right to arrange repairs:** A renter may arrange urgent repairs if they have taken reasonable steps to get the provider or agent to carry out the repairs immediately, and the renter is unable to get them to do so [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Qualified tradespeople:** Only a suitably qualified person may do repairs, both urgent and non-urgent [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). The Act defines a suitably qualified person to include a tradesperson who is registered or licensed for the work, where the work requires it [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Reporting:** You must give the owner written notice as soon as practicable after becoming aware of damage or a breakdown of facilities the owner supplied [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

**What you can do**

1. **Notify in writing now.** Send written notice of the breakdown to the owner or agent, and keep a record of the emergency contact's response that no one can attend [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
2. **Make sure the repair is urgent and qualified.** Engage a suitably qualified (registered or licensed, where required) person [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
3. **Give written notice of the repair and cost within 7 days.** You must give the owner 7 days' written notice of the repairs and their cost [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
4. **Claim reimbursement.** The owner must reimburse the reasonable cost of the repairs, or the prescribed amount if that is less, and must pay within 7 days after receiving your written notice [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The Regulations describe this as reimbursement of the reasonable cost "up to $2500" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

**If the owner refuses or the cost is too high**

You may apply to VCAT for an order requiring urgent repairs if you cannot meet the cost, the cost is more than $2500, or the owner refuses to pay for repairs you arranged [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). VCAT must hear an urgent repairs application within 2 business days after it is made [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

**What the documents don't cover**

- Whether the owner can lawfully limit repairs to their own tradespeople.
- How the Act treats a case where the owner's contact says a tradesperson will attend "later" rather than refusing outright.
- The exact cost threshold that applies to your situation, beyond the $2500 figure stated in the summaries.

**Sources:** The Residential Tenancies Act 1997 (version 115, in force from 13 October 2026) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) and the Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 (version 009, in force from 30 June 2026) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). Both are the latest versions in the retrieved documents and apply as of today. This is general information rather than legal advice; Consumer Affairs Victoria or VCAT can confirm how it applies to your circumstances.
